title: The taproom tales of the thinning at Seann Skell
summary: A coal-carrier's widow tells at the harbour-house that the children born to the departed on the far shore carry less in their hands than their parents did, and less again by the third generation. A custodian down from the vein-house answers her over a jug that the coal was never carried in the blood at all, only left behind at Muileann dhearg like a tool in an unvisited shed. Neither tale is tried against anything Seann Skell holds.

title: A third telling that silences a room
summary: A telling heard less often than the other two at Seann Skell holds that nothing thins at all: the far shore never had the coal to answer to, so its children are unremarked only for want of anything to remark them against. It is told least of the three, though it silences a hearth where the others merely fill one.

title: The vein-house's second count made
summary: Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now nine-and-thirty, carries the greater share of the vein-house's second tallying, checking the roll of the willing against the coal-right's remaining hearths column by column. The count stands where the first count of the roll had stood: one hearth in five gone from the coal-right, no more and no fewer than had sailed.

title: Donnchadh's note that the vein answers no differently
summary: Beneath the count Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets a second line unasked: that the vein answers no differently now to the hands of those who stayed than it answered before the turn, and that whatever thins in the departed's children thins on their own shore, not on this side of the water. It is carried up to Cathair dhearg with the season's reckoning.

title: Beathag reads the second count twice
summary: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill reads the vein-house's figure of one hand in five, a number she has carried unwritten in her own reckoning since the fleet sailed, and reads Donnchadh's note beneath it a second time more slowly than the first. She sets the leaf down in its place among the season's ordinary business and says no more of it that day.

title: The queen first wears the undyed wool
summary: Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes into the red hall in plain undyed wool for the first time in more than fifty years of reigning in the deep blue of the house of Dòmhnall, and takes up the day's first petition as though nothing were changed, giving the court no word for it.

title: The empty place first laid at the queen's table
summary: Beathag lays a cup, a trencher and a straight knife at the foot of her own table each evening she dines in hall, mourning her sister Mòrag with no grave to stand at and no body to wash. The court, told by the queen's steward that she mourns a sister ten years and more beyond any word reaching Cathair dhearg, does not know at first whether to speak of the place or pass it in silence.

title: The rite named an Tùrsa Geal
summary: The court names the queen's mourning an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation any household on the island that gave someone to the fleet keeps some form of the same rite unasked, undyed wool and an empty place laid with cup, trencher and straight knife, needing no crown or law behind it.

title: Donnchadh speaks of the Law's limit
summary: At a vein-house sitting called for another matter, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now its senior clerk, says plainly that the old apprenticeship built for the numbers before the turn has gone as far as the older custodians' own stretching can carry it, and that the vein-house owes itself an honest look at what remains.

title: The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days
summary: A custodian of a small old name that kept a single gallery for three generations speaks bitterly against folding his household's right into a larger kindred. An old woman of Clann Thormoid, who has buried a brother and two nephews to the roll, answers that she would sooner see her right folded into a house that can still walk its galleries than stand alone over ones it cannot serve, and the sitting turns on her answer.

title: The seven houses of custody sworn
summary: The vein-house gathers the remaining custodian households into seven kindreds large enough to answer for a share of the galleries between them: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. Their seven heads are sworn before Crom's stone, and the right to the coal passes from that year by house and no longer by apprenticeship alone.

title: Donnchadh writes the oath of the seven heads
summary: Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the seven heads' oath into the custody-book in the same plain hand he has kept his whole working life, and finds himself thinking less of the Law than of the fifth of hands the sitting never once named aloud: those fifteen years and a whole sea away, on a shore the book has no line to enter them against.

title: Death of Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill at seventy-six
summary: Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill dies at Cathair dhearg in the summer, seventy and six years old, after one-and-sixty years upon the red hall's floor, the oldest of her line and the last ruler who saw the fleet built and sent. She holds a boundary petition to its ordinary end that same morning before going to her rooms and not rising again.

title: Raghnall mac Uilleim crowned at seven-and-forty
summary: Raghnall mac Uilleim, son of Beathag and of Uilleam mac Iain, is crowned in the red hall within the month of his mother's death, seven-and-forty years old and long seated at her board. He wears a strip of undyed wool beneath his crowning colours, a thing he grew up watching his mother wear and never asked leave to wear himself.

title: The empty place laid once more at the queen's wake
summary: At the second night of Beathag's wake her steward lays the cup, trencher and straight knife once more at the foot of her table exactly as she always kept them, so that the court, passing between the small emptiness at the board's foot and the greater one at the board's head, cannot say with certainty whether the place is laid for the queen or still for the sister she mourned fifteen years across an unanswering sea.
